t: An engineer picks a resistor off a shelf and knows exactly what it will do. A biologist has never been able to do that.
Electronics works because a component behaves the same way in every circuit. Biology has never had that, and the whole of synthetic biology is an attempt to get it.
sub: That difference is why building with biology is so much harder than it sounds.
It is not that the parts are complicated. It is that they are not the same twice.

t: Making biological parts standard, so they work the same every time, is called synthetic biology.
Synthetic biology treats biological components as characterised, composable parts — the engineering discipline biology has never had.
The aspiration is abstraction: use a part by its specification without knowing its internals, as an electronic engineer does. Standard registries of characterised parts exist for exactly this.

The aspiration has proved much harder than the founders expected, and it is worth being honest about why. Parts interact through the host's shared resources — ribosomes, polymerase, energy — so adding a second circuit changes the behaviour of the first. That is a violation of the modularity assumption the whole approach rests on, and it is not a bug in any particular part.
sub: It is a good idea that biology keeps resisting.
Parts characterised in one host frequently behave differently in another, or alongside something else.
This coupling is called retroactivity or host burden, and it is the central open problem in the field.

The response has been to build insulating devices and to characterise parts in context rather than in isolation — treating context-dependence as something to be measured rather than assumed away. Twenty years in, the field is more modest and more useful than its founding manifestos.

q: Why is building with biological parts harder than with electronic ones?
Why does modularity fail in biological circuits?
Why is host burden a structural rather than incidental problem?
options: The parts affect each other through the cell they share
Nobody has written the specifications down
why: A resistor does not care what else is in the circuit. A gene does — everything in a cell shares the same machinery, so switching one thing on takes machinery away from everything else.

Parts compete for shared cellular resources, so adding one changes the behaviour of others. Modularity assumes components do not interact except through their declared connections, and in a cell they always do.

Because the resources are finite and common by construction. Every expressed construct draws on the same ribosome pool and energy budget, so coupling is a property of being in a cell rather than a flaw to be designed out. It can be reduced by insulation and by characterising in context; it cannot be eliminated.

t: The antimalarial artemisinin can now be brewed in yeast rather than farmed.

Producing artemisinic acid in engineered yeast took roughly 150 person-years and involved rebuilding a multi-step plant pathway in an organism that had never had one. It worked, and it is a fair measure of the field's real state: enormously impressive, and nothing like picking parts off a shelf.
